comparator-cascade.intro: Two 4-bit numbers A and B are compared bit by bit. Each XNOR gives xᵢ = 1 when Aᵢ = Bᵢ. Outputs: G (A > B), E (A = B), L (A < B).

elements.text: Comparing two 4-bit numbers from the MSB down

steps.caption: A = 1011 (11), B = 1001 (9). Bit 3: A3 = B3 = 1, so x3 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 2: A2 = B2 = 0, so x2 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 1: A1 = 1, B1 = 0, the first unequal bit. The term x3 x2 A1B1′ = 1 fires, so G = 1: A > B (11 > 9). Bits below 1 are ignored.
A = 0110 and B = 0110: every bit pair is equal, so all four XNORs output 1.
x3·x2·x1·x0 = 1, so E = 1 and neither G nor L fires: A = B.
A = 0101 (5), B = 0111 (7). Bit 3: A3 = B3 = 0, so x3 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 2: A2 = B2 = 1, so x2 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 1: A1 = 0, B1 = 1, the first unequal bit. The term x3 x2 A1′B1 = 1 fires, so L = 1: A < B (5 < 7). Bits below 1 are ignored.
G = A3B3′ + x3A2B2′ + x3x2A1B1′ + x3x2x1A0B0′ (xᵢ = Aᵢ ⊙ Bᵢ); L swaps A and B; E = x3x2x1x0. The MSB decides unless it ties.

set.text: G, L: first unequal bit from the top

comparator-chain.title: Two 4-bit magnitude comparators cascaded into an 8-bit comparator
comparator-chain.intro: An 8-bit comparator from two 4-bit chips. Each chip has outputs G, E, L and cascade inputs; the low chip's outputs drive the high chip's cascade inputs.

elements.text: Two 4-bit comparators cascaded into an 8-bit comparator

steps.caption: The low chip compares bits 3–0 with cascade inputs G, E, L = 0, 1, 0; its G, E, L feed the high chip's cascade inputs.
A = 0x5A, B = 0x3F. Low chip: 1010 < 1111, so it sends L = 1 to the high chip's cascade inputs.
High chip: 0101 > 0011, the nibbles differ, so it outputs G = 1 and ignores its cascade inputs: 90 > 63.
A = 0x5A, B = 0x5C. Low chip: 1010 < 1100, so it sends L = 1 to the high chip's cascade inputs.
High chip: 0101 = 0101, a tie, so it passes its cascade inputs: L = 1, the low chip's verdict. 90 < 92.
A = 0x5A, B = 0x5A. Low chip: 1010 = 1010, so it sends E = 1 to the high chip's cascade inputs.
High chip: 0101 = 0101, a tie, so it passes its cascade inputs: E = 1, the low chip's verdict. 90 = 90.
The high chip decides unless its nibbles tie; then it copies the low chip's G, E, L. The lowest chip's cascade inputs are tied to 0, 1, 0.

set.text: more chips: chain them the same way

complement-subtraction.title: Complement subtraction with the end-around carry
complement-subtraction.intro: M = 1010100 (84). We will subtract N = 1000011 (67) using only an adder and bit inversion.

elements.text: 84 − 67 with the 1's complement and the end-around carry

steps.caption: Write N = 1000011 (67) and flip every bit: N̄ = 0111100. This is the 1's complement, 2⁷ − 1 − 67 = 60.
Add M + N̄ = 1010100 + 0111100 = 1 0010000. The sum is 144 = 2⁷ + 16: a carry comes out of the top bit because M > N.
End-around carry: remove the carry (worth 2⁷) and add it back as 1 at the bottom. Removing 2⁷ leaves M − N − 1 = 16; adding 1 corrects the 'one short' of the 1's complement.
Result 0010001 = 17 = 84 − 67. Had there been no carry, the result would have been negative, with magnitude equal to the 1's complement of the sum.

complement-tree.title: Complementing an expression: swap operators, complement literals
complement-tree.intro: The expression f = (A + B′C)(A′ + D) drawn as a tree: operators inside, literals at the leaves.

elements.text: Complement = swap every operator, complement every literal

steps.caption: General De Morgan, rule 1: swap every operator, AND ↔ OR. The root AND becomes an OR, the two ORs become ANDs, and the inner AND becomes an OR.
Rule 2: complement every literal. A becomes A′, B′ becomes B, C becomes C′, A′ becomes A and D becomes D′.
Read the new tree back, keeping its grouping: the root is now an OR, so f′ = A′(B + C′) + AD′. A truth table over all 16 rows confirms it is 1 exactly where f is 0.

completeness-checklist.title: Functional completeness by Post's five classes
completeness-checklist.intro: Each row is a set of gates; each column one of Post's five closed classes.

elements.text: Post's test: a set must escape all five classes
T0: 0-preserving · T1: 1-preserving · S: self-dual · M: monotone · A: affine. ✓ = some member is outside the class.

steps.caption: NAND escapes every class: NAND(0, 0) = 1, NAND(1, 1) = 0, it is not self-dual, not monotone (0 → 1 lowers it) and not affine. Complete on its own.
AND and OR are both monotone (and 0- and 1-preserving): they can never produce a complement. Not complete.
XOR and NOT are both affine (x ⊕ y and x ⊕ 1): every circuit of them is an XOR of inputs and constants. Not complete.
AND escapes the self-dual and affine classes, NOT escapes the preserving and monotone ones: together they escape all five. Complete.
Implication escapes everything except 1-preservation (1 → 1 = 1). Not complete alone; add the constant 0 and it is.
Majority is self-dual, monotone, 0- and 1-preserving. Not complete, even with free constants (constants are monotone).
The 2:1 MUX preserves 0 and 1, so alone it is not complete; with the constants 0 and 1 it is (it then makes NOT and AND).

consensus-cells.title: The consensus theorem on the rows of a truth table
consensus-cells.intro: Three product terms over x, y, z, each drawn as the set of rows where it is 1.

elements.text: Consensus: yz is already covered by xy and x′z

steps.caption: Each cell is one row xyz of the truth table. The term xy is 1 on rows 110 and 111.
The term x′z is 1 on rows 001 and 011.
The consensus term yz is 1 on rows 011 and 111. Row 111 is already in xy (there x = 1) and row 011 is already in x′z (there x = 0).
So adding yz adds no new 1: xy + x′z + yz = xy + x′z. Whatever x is, one of the first two terms already covers yz.

set.text: yz lies inside xy + x′z, so it is redundant

converter-kmaps.title: BCD to excess-3 converter: four K-maps with don't-cares
converter-kmaps.intro: Four K-maps over the BCD digit B3 B2 B1 B0, one per excess-3 output bit E3 E2 E1 E0 (the digit plus 3). Cells 0–9 hold the outputs; cells 10–15 are don't-cares X.

elements.text: BCD → excess-3: four K-maps with don't-cares

steps.caption: Rows 10–15 are not BCD digits, so every output has an X there: six don't-cares per map that a loop may use or ignore.
The MSB E3 is 1 for digits 5–9. The octet B3 uses the Xs; quads B2B1 and B2B0 take the other 1s. E3 = B3 + B2B1 + B2B0 (3 terms).
E2 is 1 for digits 1–4 and 9: quads B2′B1 and B2′B0 use Xs, pair B2B1′B0′ (cells 4, 12) takes 4. E2 = B2′B1 + B2′B0 + B2B1′B0′ (3 terms).
E1 = 1 when B1 = B0: the left column quad B1′B0′ and the third column quad B1B0. E1 = B1′B0′ + B1B0 (2 terms).
The LSB E0 is 1 for the even digits: the octet B0′ (two outer columns) covers them all. E0 = B0′ (1 term).
All four maps are done: 17 literals in all. Without the don't-cares every map would need more or larger terms.

cyclic-map.title: The cyclic function Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) and its two minimal covers
cyclic-map.intro: Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) on a 3-variable map (rows A, columns B C).

elements.text: A cyclic function: no essential prime implicant

steps.caption: Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6): every 1 except the corners of the cube 000 and 111. Each 1 has exactly two neighbouring 1s, so it can be looped in two different pairs.
The six pairs form a ring: 1–3, 3–2, 2–6, 6–4, 4–5, 5–1. All six are prime implicants and every 1 is in two of them, so no prime implicant is essential.
Pick every other pair around the ring: B′C + A′B + AC′. Three pairs, 6 literals, every 1 covered once.
Or start one step further round: A′C + BC′ + AB′. Also three pairs and 6 literals. Two different minimal SOPs: the minimal form is not unique.

decoder-function.title: A decoder and an OR gate implementing the full-adder sum
decoder-function.intro: A 3:8 decoder with inputs A, B, C. Its outputs D1, D2, D4 and D7 feed a 4-input OR gate whose output is S.

elements.text: Decoder + OR gate: the full-adder sum Σ(1, 2, 4, 7)

steps.caption: A B C = 000: the decoder raises D0. D0 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 001: the decoder raises D1. D1 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
A B C = 010: the decoder raises D2. D2 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
A B C = 011: the decoder raises D3. D3 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 100: the decoder raises D4. D4 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
A B C = 101: the decoder raises D5. D5 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 110: the decoder raises D6. D6 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 111: the decoder raises D7. D7 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
The OR collects minterms 1, 2, 4, 7: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C, the full-adder sum. Any n-variable function is an n:2ⁿ decoder plus an OR.

decoder-lighting.title: A 3-to-8 decoder lighting one output per address
decoder-lighting.intro: A 3:8 decoder with address inputs A2 A1 A0, an enable EN, and outputs D0–D7 (active high). The address will step from 000 to 111.

elements.text: A 3:8 decoder: one output per address

steps.caption: Address A2A1A0 = 000 (= 0) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D0, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 001 (= 1) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D1, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 010 (= 2) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D2, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 011 (= 3) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D3, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 100 (= 4) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D4, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 101 (= 5) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D5, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 110 (= 6) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D6, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 111 (= 7) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D7, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Enable low: the address is 101 again, but EN = 0, so every output is 0. The enable gates all eight outputs.
EN back to 1: D5 lights again. Each output Dk is the minterm m_k of A2A1A0 ANDed with EN, so a decoder is a minterm generator.

decoder-tree.title: A 6-to-64 decoder built from 3-to-8 decoders
decoder-tree.intro: A 6:64 decoder must be built from 3:8 decoders that have an enable input. The address is A5…A0.

elements.text: A2 A1 A0 go to every leaf

steps.caption: Level 1: one 3:8 decoder takes the high address bits A5 A4 A3. Its eight outputs will not drive loads directly; they choose a leaf.
Level 2: 64 outputs need 64 / 8 = 8 leaf decoders. Each top output drives one leaf's enable, and the low bits A2 A1 A0 go to every leaf.
Count: 8 leaves + 1 top decoder = 9 decoders, and no other gates, because a 3:8 decoder has an enable input.
Address A5…A0 = 101 110: the top decoder enables leaf 5 only; that leaf decodes 110 = 6 and raises its output 6, D46.
Address A5…A0 = 000 011: the top decoder enables leaf 0 only; that leaf decodes 011 = 3 and raises its output 3, D3.
In general an n:2ⁿ decoder from k:2ᵏ decoders needs 2ⁿ / 2ᵏ leaves plus the tree above them; for 6:64 from 3:8 that is 8 + 1 = 9.

delay-models.title: The 2015 ripple adder timed under the block model and at gate level
delay-models.intro: Two timelines in microseconds for a 4-bit ripple adder with XOR = 2.4 µs and AND = OR = 1.2 µs: the top one counts each full adder as a 4.8 µs block, the bottom one follows the carries gate by gate.

elements.text: GATE 2015: block model vs gate level (µs)
block model: each FA waits for the previous one
gate level: after FA0 a carry needs only AND + OR

steps.caption: One full adder: sum = XOR + XOR = 4.8 µs, carry = XOR + AND + OR = 4.8 µs. In the block model FA0 occupies 0 … 4.8.
Block model: FA1 starts only when FA0 has finished, at 4.8 µs, and ends at 9.6.
Block model: FA2 starts only when FA1 has finished, at 9.6 µs, and ends at 14.4.
Block model: FA3 starts only when FA2 has finished, at 14.4 µs, and ends at 19.2.
Block model total: 4 × 4.8 = 19.2 µs, the official key of GATE 2015.
Gate level: c1 still needs XOR + AND + OR = 4.8 µs, because p0 = a0 ⊕ b0 must be ready first.
But p1, p2, p3 were made in parallel long ago, so each later carry costs only AND + OR = 2.4 µs: c2 at 7.2, c3 at 9.6, c4 at 12.
The last sum s3 = p3 ⊕ c3 is ready at 9.6 + 2.4 = 12 µs too. Gate level: 12 µs; block model: 19.2 µs.

set.text: gate level 12 µs vs block model 19.2 µs

demux-routing.title: A 1-to-4 demultiplexer routing the data bit
demux-routing.intro: A 1:4 DEMUX: one data input D, select lines S1 S0, and outputs Y0–Y3. The selects choose which output receives D.

elements.text: A 1:4 DEMUX sends D to the selected output

steps.caption: S1S0 = 00, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y0, so Y0 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 01, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y1, so Y1 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 10, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y2, so Y2 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 11, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y3, so Y3 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 10, D = 0: the path still leads to Y2, but it carries 0, so every output is 0.
Each output is Yk = D · m_k(S1, S0). That is a 2:4 decoder whose enable is the data line: the same chip serves as decoder or DEMUX.

design-pipeline.title: Design procedure: a word specification becomes a 3-gate circuit
design-pipeline.intro: The specification: a 4-bit BCD digit ABCD enters, and F must be 1 when the digit is 5 or more. Four stages follow: truth table, K-map, expression, circuit.

elements.text: Design procedure: “BCD digit ≥ 5” from words to gates

steps.caption: Stage 1, the truth table: F = 1 for digits 5–9, F = 0 for 0–4; the codes 1010–1111 never occur in BCD, so their F is a don't-care X.
Stage 2, the K-map: the five 1s (cells 5–9) and the six Xs (cells 10–15) are copied into a 4-variable map in Gray order.
Stage 3, grouping: the Xs let the 1s at 8 and 9 join cells 10–15 in an octet, the whole A = 1 half of the map, which reads A.
Two quads finish the cover: BC (cells 6, 7, 14, 15) and BD (cells 5, 7, 13, 15). Minimal SOP: F = A + BC + BD = A + B(C + D).
Stage 4: three gates, OR(C, D), AND with B, OR with A. No AND/OR/NOT circuit with fewer gates exists.
Test digit 6 = 0110: C + D = 1, B(C + D) = 1, so F = 1, as the table says (6 ≥ 5).
Test digit 3 = 0011: C + D = 1 but B = 0, so B(C + D) = 0 and A = 0, so F = 0 (3 < 5).

dont-care-toggle.title: Using don't-cares only where they enlarge a loop
dont-care-toggle.intro: Σm(1, 3, 7, 11, 15) + d(0, 5) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D); X marks a don't-care.

elements.text: Don't-cares: use an X only if it makes a loop bigger
Use an X only if it helps

steps.caption: f = Σm(1, 3, 7, 11, 15) + d(0, 5). The X cells may be treated as 1 or as 0, whichever gives the cheaper expression; they never need to be covered.
Column C D = 11 (m3, m7, m15, m11) is a quad of 1s: CD.
m1 is left. Without don't-cares its best loop is the pair m1, m3: A′B′D, 3 literals.
Treat X at m5 as 1: m1, m3, m5, m7 become a quad, A′D, with only 2 literals. The X at m0 would not enlarge any loop, so it stays 0 and is left out.

doubling-peel.title: Repeated doubling: 0.625 to binary
doubling-peel.intro: We will double the fraction again and again. Each integer part that pops out is one bit after the point.

elements.text: 0.625 to binary: double, peel off the integer part

steps.caption: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.25 for the next round.
0.25 × 2 = 0.5. The integer part 0 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.5 for the next round.
0.5 × 2 = 1. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0 for the next round. The fraction left is 0, so the expansion stops: 0.625 has a finite binary form.
The bits come out first-to-last from the top, so read the column downward: 0.625 = (0.101)₂ = 1/2 + 1/8.

edge-ff-timing.title: A D latch and an edge-triggered D flip-flop on the same waveforms
edge-ff-timing.intro: A D latch and a positive-edge D flip-flop share one clock and one data input D. The waveforms grow half a clock period per step (gate delays ignored); dashed lines mark the rising edges.

elements.text: Same clock, same D: a D latch and a rising-edge D flip-flop

steps.caption: Rising edge 1: the flip-flop samples D = 0 (just before the edge) and holds it. CLK = 1: D rises mid-pulse and the latch follows it.
CLK = 0: the latch is closed and holds 1; the flip-flop waits for the next edge.
Rising edge 2: the flip-flop samples D = 1 (just before the edge) and holds it. CLK = 1: D falls mid-pulse and the latch follows it.
CLK = 0: the latch is closed and holds 0; the flip-flop waits for the next edge. D changes now, but neither output moves.
Rising edge 3: the flip-flop samples D = 1 (just before the edge) and holds it. CLK = 1: the latch passes D = 1.
CLK = 0: the latch is closed and holds 1; the flip-flop waits for the next edge. D changes now, but neither output moves.
Rising edge 4: the flip-flop samples D = 0 (just before the edge) and holds it. CLK = 1: D rises mid-pulse and the latch follows it.
CLK = 0: the latch is closed and holds 1; the flip-flop waits for the next edge. D changes now, but neither output moves.
The latch followed D all through each high phase and caught the last pulse; the flip-flop stepped only at edges: 0, 1, 1, 0.

epi-highlight.title: Essential prime implicants from the 1s covered only once
epi-highlight.intro: Σm(1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Essential prime implicants: 1s with only one way out

steps.caption: f = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14) has 7 prime implicants. Count, for every 1-cell, how many of them contain it.
Three 1s lie in exactly one prime implicant: m1, m10 and m13 (shaded). Any cover must use that implicant, so it is essential.
The essential prime implicants: A′B′D, ACD′, ABC′. Draw them first.
Still uncovered: m6 and m7. Of the remaining prime implicants, A′BC covers both; A′CD or BCD′ would cover only one each and need a second term. So A′BC is the cheapest way to finish.
Minimal SOP: f = A′B′D + A′BC + ACD′ + ABC′. ABD′ is redundant: its 1s are all inside the essential ones.

equality-xnor.title: A 4-bit equality comparator from XNOR gates and an AND gate
equality-xnor.intro: Two 4-bit numbers A and B. Each bit pair goes to an XNOR gate; the four XNOR outputs go to a 4-input AND, whose output E is 1 when A = B.

elements.text: 4-bit equality: four XNORs and an AND

steps.caption: Each XNOR gives xᵢ = Aᵢ ⊙ Bᵢ, which is 1 exactly when the two bits are equal. The AND gives E = x3x2x1x0.
A = 1011, B = 1011: every pair is equal, so x3x2x1x0 = 1111 and the AND gives E = 1.
A = 1011, B = 1001: only bit 1 differs, so x1 = 0 and E = 0. One unequal pair is enough.
A = 0110, B = 1001: every pair differs, x3x2x1x0 = 0000, so E = 0.
E = (A3 ⊙ B3)(A2 ⊙ B2)(A1 ⊙ B1)(A0 ⊙ B0): n XNORs and one n-input AND test n-bit equality.

equation-sieve.title: A system of Boolean equations solved by elimination
equation-sieve.intro: All 16 assignments of P, Q, R, S (row PQRS). Each equation keeps only the rows on which its two sides are equal.

elements.text: Solving a system by striking out rows

steps.caption: Equation: P + Q = 1. At least one of P, Q is 1: the four rows with P = Q = 0 go. Twelve rows survive.
Equation: PQ = 0. P and Q are not both 1: the four rows with P = Q = 1 go. Exactly one of P, Q is 1 on the eight survivors.
Equation: Q + R = R. Q + R = R means Q = 1 forces R = 1: rows 0100 and 0101 go. Six rows survive.
Equation: P′R + S = 0. A sum equal to 0: S = 0, and P = 0 forces R = 0, which kills the remaining P = 0 rows. Two rows survive: PQRS = 1000 and 1010.

excess3-correction.title: Excess-3 addition and its ±3 correction
excess3-correction.intro: 47 and 38 in excess-3 (each digit plus 3, in 4 bits).

elements.text: Excess-3 addition 47 + 38: −3 without a carry, +3 with one

steps.caption: Units: 1010 + 1011 = 1 0101. A carry came out, so the digit sum was 10 or more: add 3. 0101 + 0011 = 1000 (excess-3 of 5), decimal carry 1.
Tens: 0111 + 0110 + carry 1 = 1110, with no carry out: the digit sum was at most 9, so subtract 3: 1110 − 0011 = 1011 (excess-3 of 8).
Why: each code carries an excess of 3, so a sum carries an excess of 6. Without a carry, remove 3 to leave a single excess of 3. With a carry, the 16 taken away already over-removed, so put 3 back.
Result 1011 1000 is excess-3 of 85 = 47 + 38.

fault-blocked.title: A stuck-at fault whose activation blocks its own propagation
fault-blocked.intro: X1 X2 X3 feed a 3-input NAND; its output and X4 feed an OR. T = AND(X3, X4). The OR output and T feed a NOR, the circuit output.

steps.caption: T = X3·X4 feeds the NOR. The fault: T stuck-at-0 (tied to ground). To activate it, the good T must be 1, so X3 = X4 = 1.
But X4 = 1 also enters the OR, and 1 is the OR's controlling value: o = 1 whatever the NAND gives, so the NOR output is 0.
X = 0 1 1 1: T = 1/0 is activated, but X4 = 1 makes o = 1, so out = 0/0 in both circuits.
X = 1 1 1 1: T = 1/0 is activated, but X4 = 1 makes o = 1, so out = 0/0 in both circuits.
X = 0 0 0 0: X3 = X4 = 0, so the good T is 0, the stuck value: not activated; out = 0/0. No test.
No input detects T s-a-0: activation (X4 = 1) blocks propagation. The answer is D, none of the above; T is redundant.

set.text: undetectable: T can be tied to 0

fault-injection.title: Injecting a stuck-at-1 fault and finding the test vector
fault-injection.intro: Two copies of the circuit p = (AB)′, f = (p·C)′. The lower copy has line p stuck at 1. Every input row is applied to both copies.

elements.text: Stuck-at-1 on line p (GATE 1994): which input detects it?

steps.caption: Rows 000–101 (A or B is 0): good p = (AB)′ = 1, the stuck value, so the fault is not activated; all 6 rows agree.
A B C = 1 1 0: good p = 0 differs from the stuck 1, but C = 0 forces f = 1 in both circuits, so nothing propagates.
A B C = 1 1 1: good p = 0, f = (0·1)′ = 1; faulty p = 1, f = (1·1)′ = 0. The outputs differ: a test.
Only 111 differs: A = B = 1 activates (good p = 0), C = 1 propagates. That one vector is the test.

fault-reconvergent.title: A stem fault whose effects reconverge and cancel
fault-reconvergent.intro: f = AB + A′C as g1 = AND(A, B), g2 = AND(A′, C), f = OR(g1, g2). Line A is stuck at 0. Each line shows good/faulty values.

elements.text: A stem fault on two reconvergent paths (A s-a-0)

steps.caption: f = AB + A′C. The stem A feeds g1 directly and g2 through an inverter. The fault: the stem A stuck-at-0, so both branches see 0.
The obvious test, A B C = 1 1 1: activate A (good 1) and open g1 (B = 1). But C = 1 also opens g2 to the faulty A′ = 1.
g1 = 1/0 and g2 = 0/1: the error and its complement reach the OR together, so f = 1/1. The two paths cancel; 111 is not a test.
A B C = 1 1 0: only one path is open, through g1 (C = 0 closes g2). f = 1/0: the outputs differ, a test.
A B C = 1 0 1: only one path is open, through g2 (B = 0 closes g1). f = 0/1: the outputs differ, a test.
∂f/∂A = B ⊕ C, so the stem tests are A = 1, B ≠ C: 101 and 110 only. The branch into g1 alone has tests 110 and 111.

feedback-stability.title: Stable states of a feedback loop, found by cutting it
feedback-stability.intro: A combinational block f(a, b, Q) = aQ + ab + bQ with its output Q fed back to its own input. The loop is cut, Q in is assumed 0 or 1, and Q out is compared with it.

elements.text: Cut the loop: which values of Q reproduce themselves?
Cut the loop and test Q
the loop is cut: assume Q in, compute Q out

steps.caption: a = 0, b = 0: assume Q in = 0; the block gives Q out = 0, the same, so Q = 0 is stable.
a = 0, b = 0: assume Q in = 1; the block gives Q out = 0, different, so Q = 1 cannot last.
a b = 00: stable Q = 0, so the loop acts as constant 0.
a = 0, b = 1: assume Q in = 0; the block gives Q out = 0, the same, so Q = 0 is stable.
a = 0, b = 1: assume Q in = 1; the block gives Q out = 1, the same, so Q = 1 is stable.
a b = 01: stable Q = 0 and 1, so the loop acts as memory (it keeps the old Q).
a = 1, b = 0: assume Q in = 0; the block gives Q out = 0, the same, so Q = 0 is stable.
a = 1, b = 0: assume Q in = 1; the block gives Q out = 1, the same, so Q = 1 is stable.
a b = 10: stable Q = 0 and 1, so the loop acts as memory (it keeps the old Q).
a = 1, b = 1: assume Q in = 0; the block gives Q out = 1, different, so Q = 0 cannot last.
a = 1, b = 1: assume Q in = 1; the block gives Q out = 1, the same, so Q = 1 is stable.
a b = 11: stable Q = 1, so the loop acts as constant 1.
The loop holds a bit when a ≠ b, and is forced to a = b otherwise: the 1991 table 0, Q, Q, 1.

ff-conversion.title: Converting flip-flops: a JK flip-flop from a D flip-flop
ff-conversion.intro: The conversion method for a JK flip-flop built from a D flip-flop: the JK characteristic table, the D column from the D excitation table, and the K-map of D.

elements.text: Building a JK flip-flop from a D flip-flop
JK from D, step by step

steps.caption: JK = 00 is 'hold', so from Q = 0 and Q = 1 the JK goes to 0 and 1.
JK = 01 is 'reset', so from Q = 0 and Q = 1 the JK goes to 0 and 0.
JK = 10 is 'set', so from Q = 0 and Q = 1 the JK goes to 1 and 1.
JK = 11 is 'toggle', so from Q = 0 and Q = 1 the JK goes to 1 and 0.
A D flip-flop goes wherever D tells it, so its excitation is simply D = Q⁺: the D column copies the Q⁺ column.
Place the D column in a K-map with Q down the side and JK across in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10.
Row Q = 0 has 1s under JK = 11 and 10, the columns where J = 1: the group J·Q̄ (set or toggle from 0).
Row Q = 1: cells 00 and 10 are adjacent (wrap-around), drawn as one group open at both map edges; K = 0 there: K̄Q.
So D = JQ̄ + K̄Q, the JK characteristic equation itself: with a D flip-flop, D is always the wanted Q⁺.

set.text: check: J = K = 1 gives D = Q̄

five-var-map.title: A five-variable K-map as two four-variable maps
five-var-map.intro: f(A, B, C, D, E) = Σm(0, 2, 7, 8, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 18, 24, 26, 27, 30, 31), drawn as an A = 0 map and an A = 1 map (rows B C, columns D E).

elements.text: Five variables: two 4-variable maps, A = 0 and A = 1

steps.caption: A 5-variable map is two 4-variable maps (rows B C, columns D E), one for A = 0 and one for A = 1. Inside each map the usual neighbours apply; in addition every cell is adjacent to the cell in the same position of the other map (they differ only in A).

set.text: same position in the other map = neighbour

steps.caption: The four corner cells of each map (C = 0, E = 0) are 1s in both maps. In each map they form a corner quad, and the two quads face each other: one group of 8 = 2³ cells, so 5 − 3 = 2 literals: C′E′.
Rows B C = 11 and 10, columns D E = 11 and 10 (B = 1, D = 1) are 1s in both maps: another octet across the maps, BD.
Remaining: m7 (00111) in the A = 0 map only. Its twin m23 is 0, so the loop cannot cross to A = 1; inside its own map it pairs with m15: A′CDE (4 literals).

set.text: twin cell is 0: the pair stays in one map

fixed-point-bits.title: Bit weights in a 5.3 fixed-point byte
fixed-point-bits.intro: Eight bit cells b7 to b0 with the binary point between b3 and b2. Weights above the point are 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; below it ½, ¼, ⅛. The pattern 01011.010 is 8 + 2 + 1 + ¼ = 11.25. The format covers 0 to 31.875 in steps of ⅛.

elements.text: Unsigned 5.3 fixed point: b₇ … b₃ . b₂ b₁ b₀
range 0 … 31.875 in steps of ⅛ (2⁸ = 256 values)

fixed-point-ruler.title: Fixed point: the range–resolution trade-off
fixed-point-ruler.intro: A number line from 0 to 16 with sixteen tick marks, one for each 4-bit pattern. Each step moves the binary point one place left.

elements.text: 4 bits, point moved: range shrinks, steps get finer

steps.caption: With 0 fraction bits (4.0 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 1 from 0 to 15: resolution 1, largest value 15 = 2⁴ − 1.
With 1 fraction bit (3.1 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.5 from 0 to 7.5: resolution 0.5, largest value 7.5 = 2³ − 0.5.
With 2 fraction bits (2.2 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.25 from 0 to 3.75: resolution 0.25, largest value 3.75 = 2² − 0.25.
With 3 fraction bits (1.3 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.125 from 0 to 1.875: resolution 0.125, largest value 1.875 = 2¹ − 0.125.
The count of values never changes: n bits always give 2ⁿ = 16 patterns. Moving the point only trades range for resolution.

fp-align-add.title: Floating-point addition: align, add, normalise, round
fp-align-add.intro: Two numbers in a toy format with 4 fraction bits: A = 7 = 1.1100 × 2² and B = 1.625 = 1.1010 × 2⁰.

steps.caption: Write both significands with their hidden 1 and two extra guard positions. A = 1.1100 × 2², B = 1.1010 × 2⁰. The exponents differ by 2.
Align: shift the smaller number right by 2 and raise its exponent to 2. B becomes 0.0110 × 2², and the bits shifted out (1 0) land in the guard and round positions instead of being lost.
Add the aligned significands: 1.1100 00 + 0.0110 10 = 10.0010 10. The sum overflowed into a second integer bit.
Normalise: 10.0010 10 has two bits before the point, so shift right by 1 and add 1 to the exponent: 1.0001 010 × 2³. The bit shifted out joins the extra bits: G = 0, R = 1.
Round to nearest even: the guard bit is 0, so the extra bits are less than half an ulp and are dropped. Result 1.0001 × 2³ = 8.5.

set.text: stored 8.5; exact sum 8.625 (error 0.125, under half an ulp = 0.25)

frequency-divider.title: Frequency division in a 3-bit ripple counter
frequency-divider.intro: The clock and the outputs Q0, Q1 and Q2 of a 3-bit negative-edge ripple counter (delays ignored), one clock period per step; then each output's period is marked.

elements.text: A ripple counter is a chain of divide-by-two stages

steps.caption: Clock period T. Q0 toggles at every falling edge of CLK; Q1 at every falling edge of Q0; Q2 at every falling edge of Q1.
Falling edge 1: the count becomes 001 = 1.
Falling edge 2: the count becomes 010 = 2. Q0 has fallen, so Q1 toggles too.
Falling edge 3: the count becomes 011 = 3.
Falling edge 4: the count becomes 100 = 4. Q0 has fallen, so Q1 toggles too. Q1 has fallen as well: Q2 toggles.
Falling edge 5: the count becomes 101 = 5.
Falling edge 6: the count becomes 110 = 6. Q0 has fallen, so Q1 toggles too.
Falling edge 7: the count becomes 111 = 7.
Falling edge 8: the count becomes 000 = 0. Q0 has fallen, so Q1 toggles too. Q1 has fallen as well: Q2 toggles.
Falling edge 9: the count becomes 001 = 1.
Falling edge 10: the count becomes 010 = 2. Q0 has fallen, so Q1 toggles too.
Falling edge 11: the count becomes 011 = 3.
Falling edge 12: the count becomes 100 = 4. Q0 has fallen, so Q1 toggles too. Q1 has fallen as well: Q2 toggles.
Q0 repeats every 2 clock periods: period 2T, frequency f/2.
Q1 repeats every 4 clock periods: period 4T, frequency f/4. Each stage halves the frequency of the one before.
Q2 repeats every 8 clock periods: period 8T, frequency f/8. The third stage is Q2, at f/8.
Stage i of a ripple counter runs at f/2^(i+1); an n-bit counter's last stage gives f/2^n, here f/8 with a 50% duty cycle.

fsm-to-circuit.title: The GATE 2001 machine as a JK circuit
fsm-to-circuit.intro: Left (top on phones): the 4-state Mealy state table, entries next state/output. Right (below): the same table in bits after the assignment A = 00, B = 01, C = 10, D = 11, with the JK excitation columns; the equations appear underneath.

elements.text: From state table to JK equations (GATE 2001 machine)

steps.caption: The 2001 machine: A, B copy the input, C, D complement it. B remembers 'last bit 0', D 'last bit 1'. Arcs are next/output.
Assign A = 00, B = 01, C = 10, D = 11: Q1 is the mode (0 copy, 1 complement), Q0 the 'one more of the same bit ends the mode' flag.
Rewrite the rows of A (00) and B (01) in bits: next state NS and output z read straight from the state table.
Rewrite the rows of C (10) and D (11) in bits: next state NS and output z read straight from the state table.
J1, K1 from the JK excitation table: J1 matters only where Q1 = 0, K1 only where Q1 = 1. The single 1s give J1 = Q0x′, K1 = Q0x.
J0 is 1 in rows 00 with x = 0 and 10 with x = 1: J0 = Q1x + Q1′x′ (Q1 XNOR x). Every K0 entry is 1 or ×, so K0 = 1.
Output: z = x in the copy mode (Q1 = 0) and x′ in the complement mode (Q1 = 1), so z = x ⊕ Q1. It depends on x: a Mealy output.
Check: the circuit, simulated on the 2001 example 101100 01001011 011, outputs 101100 10110100 011, exactly as asked.

full-adder-from-has.title: A full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate
full-adder-from-has.intro: Inputs A, B and Cin. HA1 adds A and B; HA2 adds HA1's sum and Cin; an OR gate combines the two half-adder carries into Cout.

elements.text: A full adder from two half adders and an OR gate

steps.caption: HA1 adds A and B: its XOR gives the partial sum p = A ⊕ B, its AND gives g = A·B (a carry made here).
HA2 adds p and Cin: S = p ⊕ Cin is the full sum, t = p·Cin is a carry made by passing Cin along.
The OR merges the two possible carries: Cout = g + t = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B).
A, B, Cin = 1, 1, 1: p = 0, g = 1, t = 0; S = 1, Cout = 1 (1 + 1 + 1 = 3); both carries can never be 1 together.
A, B, Cin = 1, 0, 1: p = 1, g = 0, t = 1; S = 0, Cout = 1 (1 + 0 + 1 = 2); both carries can never be 1 together.
A, B, Cin = 0, 1, 0: p = 1, g = 0, t = 0; S = 1, Cout = 0 (0 + 1 + 0 = 1); no carry is made.
A, B, Cin = 1, 1, 0: p = 0, g = 1, t = 0; S = 0, Cout = 1 (1 + 1 + 0 = 2); both carries can never be 1 together.

function-count.title: Counting Boolean functions: one free output bit per row
function-count.intro: A Boolean function is completely described by its output column. Count the columns.

elements.text: How many Boolean functions of n variables?

steps.caption: One variable: 2 rows. Each row's output is an independent choice of 0 or 1, so there are 2 × 2 = 2² = 4 functions: 0, x, x′ and 1.

set.text: a function = one output bit per row

steps.caption: Two variables: 4 rows, so 2⁴ = 16 functions, the sixteen of Lesson 1.
Three variables: 8 rows, so 2⁸ = 256 functions. In general n variables give 2ⁿ rows and 2^(2ⁿ) functions; for n = 4 that is 65 536.

gate-symbols.title: The seven logic gates with their truth tables filling row by row
gate-symbols.intro: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, each fed by the inputs A and B (NOT reads only A). The strip under each gate will hold its output for rows 00, 01, 10 and 11.

elements.text: The seven gates, row by row
The seven gates, row by row

steps.caption: Row 0: A = 0, B = 0. Outputs: NOT 1, AND 0, OR 0, NAND 1, NOR 1, XOR 0, XNOR 1.
Row 1: A = 0, B = 1. Outputs: NOT 1, AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.
Row 2: A = 1, B = 0. Outputs: NOT 0, AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.
Row 3: A = 1, B = 1. Outputs: NOT 0, AND 1, OR 1, NAND 0, NOR 0, XOR 0, XNOR 1.
Each gate's four outputs, read top to bottom, are its truth table: NOT 1100 (it reads only A), AND 0001, OR 0111, NAND 1110, NOR 1000, XOR 0110, XNOR 1001.

glitch-timing.title: Timing diagram of the X·X′ glitch
glitch-timing.intro: A signal X feeds an AND gate directly and through an inverter with a delay of 1 time unit. The AND gate is ideal (no delay).

elements.text: A glitch from a slow inverter: Y = X·X′

steps.caption: X rises at t = 2 and falls at t = 6. Logically Y = X·X′ is always 0.
The inverter takes one time unit, so X′ falls only at t = 3 and rises only at t = 7.
Between t = 2 and t = 3 both AND inputs are 1, so Y pulses to 1 for exactly the inverter delay: a static-0 hazard (a glitch).

set.text: 1-pulse of width = inverter delay on the rising edge

steps.caption: On the falling edge (t = 6 to 7) X is already 0 while X′ is still 0, so the AND sees 0, 0 and Y stays 0. The glitch appears only after X rises.

set.text: no glitch on the falling edge

gradual-underflow.title: Gradual underflow: denormals fill the hole around zero
gradual-underflow.intro: The values from 0 to 1 of a toy IEEE-style format with a 3-bit exponent (bias 3) and 2 fraction bits. At first only the normal numbers are drawn.

elements.text: A toy float (3-bit exponent, 2 fraction bits) between 0 and 1

steps.caption: With normal numbers only, the smallest positive value is 1/4 (1.00 × 2⁻²) and the next one down is 0. Just above 1/4 the values are 1/16 apart, but below it there is a hole four times wider.
Take x = 5/16 and y = 4/16, two different normal numbers. Their difference 1/16 falls in the hole, so a flush-to-zero machine returns x − y = 0 even though x ≠ y.
Denormals use the exponent field 0 with no hidden 1: 0.f × 2⁻², giving 1/16, 2/16 and 3/16. They fill the hole with the same 1/16 spacing as the first normal binade.

set.label: with denormals: evenly spaced down to 0

steps.caption: Now x − y = 1/16 is the denormal 0.01 × 2⁻², stored exactly. With denormals, x ≠ y always gives x − y ≠ 0.
The largest denormal, 3/16, is exactly one step below the smallest normal, 1/4. In IEEE single precision the same picture holds with 2⁻¹⁴⁹ steps up to 2⁻¹²⁶.

gray-converter.title: Binary to Gray and Gray to binary converters
gray-converter.intro: First: a binary → Gray converter (three independent XORs). Second: a Gray → binary converter (a ripple of XORs). The input is 1011.

elements.text: Binary → Gray and back, bit by bit (input 1011)

steps.caption: The binary input b3 b2 b1 b0 = 1011 enters. Each Gray bit XORs two neighbouring binary bits; the three XORs work at once.
g3 = b3 = 1: the MSB is copied unchanged.
g2 = b3 ⊕ b2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: the bits differ, so the Gray bit is 1.
g1 = b2 ⊕ b1 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1: the bits differ, so the Gray bit is 1.
g0 = b1 ⊕ b0 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: the bits are equal, so the Gray bit is 0.
The Gray code of 1011 is 1110. To convert back, the Gray bits g3 g2 g1 g0 = 1110 enter the second circuit.
b3 = g3 = 1: the MSB is copied again.
b2 = b3 ⊕ g2 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: each binary bit needs the binary bit just found, so the decode ripples from the MSB down.
b1 = b2 ⊕ g1 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1: each binary bit needs the binary bit just found, so the decode ripples from the MSB down.
b0 = b1 ⊕ g0 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: each binary bit needs the binary bit just found, so the decode ripples from the MSB down.
The ripple returns 1011, the original input. Binary → Gray needs no chain (each XOR is independent); Gray → binary is a chain of 3 XORs.

gray-reflect.title: Reflected Gray code, built by mirroring
gray-reflect.intro: The 1-bit Gray code, 0 and 1. Longer codes will be built to its right, each from the one before.

steps.caption: Start with the 1-bit Gray code: 0, 1. The two codes differ in one bit.
Copy the list, then append its mirror image (1, 0) underneath. Put 0 in front of the top half and 1 in front of the bottom half: 00, 01, 11, 10.
Do it again: the 2-bit list, then its mirror, with prefixes 0 and 1. The result is the 3-bit reflected Gray code: 000 001 011 010 110 111 101 100.
Across the mirror line the two neighbours are the same code with only the new front bit changed (010 → 110). And the last code 100 differs from the first 000 in one bit too, so the list wraps round.

gray-wheel.title: Rotary encoder disc in Gray code
gray-wheel.intro: A disc cut into 8 sectors and 3 rings. Reading clockwise from the top, the sectors are coded 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100. At every boundary between neighbouring sectors only one ring changes between clear and shaded, so a sensor sitting on a boundary can misread at most one bit and is never more than one position wrong.

elements.text: inner ring = first bit, outer ring = last bit; shaded = 1

gray-xor-ladder.title: The XOR ladder between binary and Gray
gray-xor-ladder.intro: The binary number 1011 on top and an empty Gray row underneath.

elements.text: Binary → Gray: XOR each bit with its left neighbour

steps.caption: The first Gray bit is the first binary bit, copied: 1.
The second Gray bit (from the left) = first binary bit ⊕ second binary bit = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
The third Gray bit (from the left) = second binary bit ⊕ third binary bit = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
The fourth Gray bit (from the left) = third binary bit ⊕ fourth binary bit = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
So binary 1011 (eleven) has Gray code 1110. In one line: Gray = b ⊕ (b shifted right by 1).
Going back, each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits from the left down to it, a running XOR: Gray 101100 gives binary 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1 = 110111.

grouping-slider.title: Grouping bits into octal and hex digits
grouping-slider.intro: The seven bits 1011010. The red dot marks the radix point at the right end. Dashed cells on the left are padding zeros that will appear when a group runs short.

elements.text: Grouping the bits of (1011010)₂ from the right

steps.caption: Start at the radix point (here, just right of the last bit) and cut off three bits: 010. Three bits make one octal digit, and 010 is 2.
The next three bits to the left, 011, are the octal digit 3.
Only one bit, 1, is left. Pad it on the left with two zeros (that adds nothing to the value) to make 001 = 1.
Read the groups left to right: (1011010)₂ = (132)₈. Check: 64 + 24 + 2 = 90.
Now regroup in fours for hexadecimal, again starting at the point: 1010 is A.
The last three bits 101 need one padding zero: 0101 = 5. So (1011010)₂ = (5A)₁₆ = 5·16 + 10 = 90.

half-adder-design.title: The half adder from its truth table
half-adder-design.intro: A half adder adds two bits A and B. Its truth table has four rows and two output columns, S and C.

elements.text: Designing the half adder: table, equations, gates

steps.caption: Adding two bits A + B gives 0, 1 or 2, so we need two outputs: the sum bit S (weight 1) and the carry C (weight 2).
S column: S = 1 exactly when one input is 1 (rows 01 and 10). That is the odd function: S = A ⊕ B.
C column: a carry appears only for 1 + 1 = 10 (binary), row 11. So C = A·B.
Two gates realise the two equations: an XOR for S and an AND for C, both fed by A and B.
Row A = 0, B = 0: 0 + 0 = 0, so S = 0 and C = 0 (binary 00).
Row A = 0, B = 1: 0 + 1 = 1, so S = 1 and C = 0 (binary 01).
Row A = 1, B = 0: 1 + 0 = 1, so S = 1 and C = 0 (binary 01).
Row A = 1, B = 1: 1 + 1 = 2, so S = 0 and C = 1 (binary 10).

hamming-74-venn.title: Hamming (7,4) as three overlapping parity circles
hamming-74-venn.intro: Three overlapping circles named 1, 2 and 4. The seven regions hold bit positions 1 to 7: position 7 is in all three circles, 3 in circles 1 and 2, 5 in circles 1 and 4, 6 in circles 2 and 4, and 1, 2, 4 each in one circle only. The data bits 1, 0, 1, 1 sit in positions 3, 5, 6, 7.

steps.caption: Each parity bit makes its circle hold an even number of 1s. Circle 1 holds positions 3, 5, 7 = 1, 0, 1: two 1s already, so p1 = 0.
Circle 2 holds positions 3, 6, 7 = 1, 1, 1: three 1s, so p2 = 1 to make four.
Circle 4 holds positions 5, 6, 7 = 0, 1, 1: two 1s, so p4 = 0. The codeword (positions 1–7) is 0110011.
Noise flips position 6 (1 → 0). The received word is 0110001.
Recount each circle. Circle 1 is still even (it does not contain position 6). Circles 2 and 4 are now odd: they fail.
Add the numbers of the failing circles: 2 + 4 = 6. The only position inside circles 2 and 4 but outside circle 1 is 6, so flip it back. Syndrome 6, corrected word 0110011.

hazard-glitch.title: A static-1 hazard in AB + A′C and the consensus term that removes it
hazard-glitch.intro: f = AB + A′C built as AND–OR with an inverter on A (delay 1); B and C are held at 1 while A falls at t = 3.

elements.text: A static-1 hazard and the consensus fix

steps.caption: f = AB + A′C with B = C = 1, so logically f = A + A′ = 1 whatever A does. A falls at t = 3; the inverter makes A′ rise one unit later, at t = 4.
AB follows A and falls at t = 3; A′C follows A′ and rises only at t = 4. For one time unit both AND outputs are 0.
So f = AB + A′C drops to 0 between t = 3 and t = 4: a static-1 hazard. On the map the two 1-cells m7 (A = 1) and m3 (A = 0) are adjacent but lie in different loops.
Add the consensus term BC, the loop that contains both m3 and m7. With B = C = 1 it is 1 throughout, so f = AB + A′C + BC stays 1: the hazard is gone, at the cost of one more AND gate.

set.text: add BC: every adjacent pair of 1s now shares a loop

hex-nibble-table.title: The sixteen hex digits as 4-bit groups, with their count of 1s
hex-nibble-table.intro: Two tables. Left: hex digits 0 to 7, right: 8 to F. Each row gives the digit, its four bits, how many of those bits are 1, and its decimal value. For example 7 is 0111 with three 1s, and F is 1111 with four 1s.

horner-chain.title: Horner's chain: (257)₈ to decimal
horner-chain.intro: Start with a running total of 0. Each arrow will multiply the total by the base 8 and add one digit.

elements.text: Horner's chain for (257)₈: multiply by 8, add the next digit

steps.caption: Take the running total 0, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 2: 0 × 8 + 2 = 2.
Take the running total 2, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 5: 2 × 8 + 5 = 21.
Take the running total 21, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 7: 21 × 8 + 7 = 175.
Every digit has been used, so the last total is the value: (257)₈ = 175. The same total comes from 2·64 + 5·8 + 7, but without writing any powers.

ieee-encode.title: Decimal to IEEE-754: encoding 13.625
ieee-encode.intro: We will turn 13.625 into a 32-bit single-precision word, one decision at a time.

steps.caption: Step 1, the sign: 13.625 is positive, so the sign bit is 0.
Step 2, the integer part in binary: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 1101₂.
Step 3, the fraction part by repeated doubling: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25 (bit 1), 0.25 × 2 = 0.5 (bit 0), 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 (bit 1). So 0.625 = 0.101₂, and it terminates.
Step 4, normalise: move the point 3 places left so exactly one 1 is before it. 1101.101₂ = 1.101101₂ × 2³.
Step 5, bias the exponent: e = 3 + 127 = 130 = 10000010₂.
Step 6, the fraction field holds the bits after the point (the leading 1 is hidden): 101101, padded with 17 zeros to 23 bits.
Step 7, assemble sign | exponent | fraction into 32 bits.
Step 8, regroup the 32 bits in fours to get hex: 0x415A0000. Decoding it gives 1.703125 × 8 = 13.625 exactly, because 13.625 = 109/8 has a power-of-two denominator.

ieee-layout.title: IEEE-754 single and double layouts
ieee-layout.intro: The 32 bits of −6.75 in single precision, split into a 1-bit sign (red), an 8-bit exponent (blue) and a 23-bit fraction (green).

elements.text: IEEE-754 layouts: −6.75 in single, then in double

steps.caption: The sign bit (bit 31) comes first. It is 1, so the number is negative. The significand is stored as a magnitude: sign-magnitude, not 2's complement.
Bits 30–23 hold the biased exponent e = 10000001 = 129. Subtracting the bias 127 gives the true exponent E = 2.
Bits 22–0 hold the fraction f = 1011 followed by zeros. The leading 1 of the significand is hidden, so the significand is 1.1011₂ = 1.6875.
Put it together: (−1)¹ × 1.1011₂ × 2² = −110.11₂ = −6.75. In hex the word is 0xC0D80000.
Double precision keeps the same three fields, only wider: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit exponent with bias 1023, and a 52-bit fraction.
The same −6.75 as a double: the true exponent is still 2, so e = 1025; the fraction 1011 is padded with 48 zeros. The word is 0xC01B000000000000.

ieee-special-values.title: IEEE-754 special values
ieee-special-values.intro: The five ways IEEE-754 single precision reads a word, chosen by the exponent field and whether the fraction is zero.

elements.text: How IEEE-754 single precision reads the exponent field

steps.caption: 0x00000000 is +0 and 0x80000000 is −0. They compare equal, but 1/(+0) = +∞ and 1/(−0) = −∞.
0x00400000 has e = 0 and f = 100…0: a denormal, 0.1₂ × 2⁻¹²⁶ = 2⁻¹²⁷. No hidden 1, and the exponent is fixed at −126.
Every field from 1 to 254 is an ordinary number with a hidden 1: 0x3F800000 has e = 127, so it is 1.0.
0x7F800000 is +∞ and 0xFF800000 is −∞: the results of overflow or of dividing a non-zero number by zero.
0x7FC00000 has e = 255 and a non-zero fraction: NaN, from 0/0, ∞ − ∞ or √−1. NaN is unequal even to itself.
Only the two end fields are special. The 254 fields in between hold every normal number, from 2⁻¹²⁶ up to about 3.4 × 10³⁸.

implication-table.title: The implication table of the GATE 1996 machine
implication-table.intro: A four-state Mealy machine. Each cell of the staircase is a pair of states; cells with different output rows are crossed first, then every cell that implies a crossed cell, until a pass crosses nothing.

elements.text: The implication table of the GATE 1996 machine

steps.caption: One cell per pair of states: 4 states give 6 cells. A pair stays uncrossed until something proves it different.
Pass 0: D's output row is 11, the others' is 01, so the three cells of row D are crossed at once.
Fill the other cells with implied pairs: A–B needs AD and BC, A–C needs AD, B–C needs only BC, itself.
Pass 1: A–B lists AD, which is crossed, so A–B is crossed: if A ≡ B then A ≡ D, which is false.
Pass 1: A–C lists AD, which is crossed, so A–C is crossed: if A ≡ C then A ≡ D, which is false.
B–C lists only itself, which is not crossed. Pass 2 crosses nothing more, so the table is finished.
Survivor B–C: B ≡ C. Classes {A} {B,C} {D}: 3 states (GATE 1996), as partition refinement found.

kmap-adjacency.title: Neighbours of a cell on a 4-variable K-map, through the edges too
kmap-adjacency.intro: A 4-variable map with every cell numbered (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Neighbours on a K-map, edges included

steps.caption: m5 = 0101. Its four neighbours are the cells above, below, left and right: m1, m4, m7, m13. Each differs from 0101 in exactly one bit.
m8 = 1000 sits on the bottom-left corner. Its neighbours are m10 (right edge, through the wrap), m0 (top row, through the wrap), m9 and m12: still exactly one bit different each.
m2 = 0010 is in the top row, last column. Its neighbours: m0 (left end of the same row, through the wrap), m3, m6 and m10 (bottom row, through the wrap).

set.text: roll the map: left meets right

steps.caption: Picture the map rolled into a tube (left edge glued to right) and the tube bent into a ring (top glued to bottom): a torus. On that surface every cell has exactly four neighbours, and they are exactly the minterms one bit away.

kmap-checkerboard.title: The checkerboard K-map of 4-variable parity
kmap-checkerboard.intro: A 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D) with 1s on the odd-parity minterms.

elements.text: The checkerboard: parity cannot be grouped

steps.caption: The 1s are the minterms with an odd number of 1 bits: 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14. They form a checkerboard.
Every neighbour of a 1 is a 0: moving to a neighbour flips one bit, which changes the parity. Here m1 = 0001 and its neighbours m0, m3, m5, m9 all have an even number of 1s.

set.text: each neighbour flips one bit → parity flips

steps.caption: So no two 1s are adjacent: every prime implicant is a single minterm, and the minimal SOP has all 8 minterms (32 literals). The compact form is the XOR A ⊕ B ⊕ C ⊕ D.
A partial checkerboard, where only some variables alternate, does group: 1s where B = D form the two quads B′D′ (corners) and BD (centre), so f = B′D′ + BD = (B ⊕ D)′.

kmap-corner-quad.title: The corner quad B′D′ on a 4-variable K-map
kmap-corner-quad.intro: A 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D) with 1s in the four corner cells.

elements.text: The four corners form one group
The four corners are one group

steps.caption: The 1s are the four corners: m0 = 0000, m2 = 0010, m8 = 1000, m10 = 1010. They look as far apart as cells can be.
Across the left/right edge: m0 and m2 differ only in C (0000, 0010), and so do m8 and m10. Across the top/bottom edge: m0 and m8 differ only in A, m2 and m10 too.
So the four corners are a 2 × 2 block on the torus: one group of 4, drawn as four corner pieces that reach outward through the edges.
Inside the group A and C both change; B = 0 and D = 0 never change. A group of 4 = 2² cells keeps 4 − 2 = 2 literals: B′D′.

set.text: A and C change: they drop

kmap-gray-layout.title: Placing minterms on a 4-variable K-map in Gray order
kmap-gray-layout.intro: An empty 4-variable map. Rows will be labelled by A B and columns by C D. Minterm m has A as its most significant bit.

steps.caption: Columns are labelled by C D and rows by A B, each in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10: the third label is 11, not 10, so that every step along an axis flips exactly one bit.
Row A B = 00: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 0, 1, 3, 2. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
Row A B = 01: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 4, 5, 7, 6. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
Row A B = 11: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 12, 13, 15, 14. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
Row A B = 10: minterm number = 4·(A B) + (C D), so the row reads 8, 9, 11, 10. The last two are swapped compared with counting order, because the columns are in Gray order.
The finished map, cell numbers 0 1 3 2 / 4 5 7 6 / 12 13 15 14 / 8 9 11 10. Any two cells side by side (or at opposite ends of a row or column) differ in exactly one variable.

set.text: Memorise the pattern: swap the last two of every row, then the last two rows.

kmap-grouping.title: Grouping a 4-variable K-map: an octet and two wrap-around quads
kmap-grouping.intro: Σm(0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Grouping the 1s: biggest legal loops, fewest of them

steps.caption: Eleven 1s to cover. Look for the largest possible groups first, but make sure every loop is a rectangle of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells (wrap-around allowed).
The first two columns (C D = 00 and 01) are all 1s: an octet. C is 0 in both columns; A, B and D all change. 8 = 2³ cells keep 4 − 3 = 1 literal: C′.

Still uncovered: m2, m6 and m14 (column C D = 10). Start with m2 and m6: they join m0 and m4 in the first column through the left/right wrap: a quad in rows A B = 00, 01. A = 0 and D = 0 stay fixed: A′D′.
Still uncovered: m14. Its biggest loop also wraps: m12, m14 with m4, m6 in rows A B = 01, 11. B = 1 and D = 0 stay fixed: BD′.
Every 1 is now inside a loop, and no loop can be bigger or dropped. Minimal SOP: f = C′ + A′D′ + BD′, with 5 literals.

kmap-pos-zeros.title: Minimal POS by grouping the 0s of a K-map
kmap-pos-zeros.intro: F(P, Q, R, S) = PQ + P′QR + P′QR′S on a map with rows P Q and columns R S; the 0s are shown.

elements.text: POS: loop the 0s, read sum terms

steps.caption: F = PQ + P′QR + P′QR′S has 9 zeros: m0, m1, m2, m3, m4, m8, m9, m10, m11. For a product of sums, loop the 0s exactly as you would loop 1s.
Rows P Q = 00 and 10 are all 0s: an octet of 0s. Q = 0 throughout. A group of 0s is read as a sum term with each fixed variable written so that it is 0 on the group: Q = 0 gives the factor (Q).
Left: m4 = 0100. Pair it with m0 (column R S = 00, rows 00 and 01): P = 0, R = 0, S = 0 are fixed, so the factor is (P + R + S) (a 0 bit gives the plain letter).
Minimal POS: F = (Q)(P + R + S), 4 literals. The minimal SOP, QS + QR + PQ, needs 6. Here the POS is cheaper.

kmap-trap-labels.title: A K-map printed with binary-order labels, re-drawn in Gray order
kmap-trap-labels.intro: A 3-variable map with rows A = 0, 1 and columns labelled B C = 00, 01, 10, 11 as printed in a GATE paper. Each row reads 1 0 0 1.

elements.text: Trap: a map printed in binary order

steps.caption: The columns are labelled 00, 01, 10, 11: plain counting order, not Gray order. Between the 2nd and 3rd columns two bits change (01 → 10), and the two end columns (00 and 11) are not neighbours either.
The tempting mistake: treat the end columns as a wrap-around group of four 1s and write C′. On this map the ends differ in two bits, so that loop is illegal.

set.text: wrap loop of the ends: illegal

steps.caption: Re-draw the columns in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10: the column of 1s labelled 11 moves to the third place. Now the 1s are in columns 00 and 11, which are not adjacent.
Two vertical pairs: B = C = 0 gives B′C′, B = C = 1 gives BC (A changes in both, so it drops). f = B′C′ + BC = (B ⊕ C)′, the XNOR of B and C.

law-cards.title: Proving Boolean laws by truth table
law-cards.intro: Three laws, each proved by listing every case: idempotence, absorption, and the redundant-literal rule.

steps.caption: Card 1. Idempotence: x + x = x and x·x = x: list every row of the variables (2 rows).

set.text: Idempotence: x + x = x and x·x = x

steps.caption: Fill each column from the definitions. The highlighted columns x, x+x, xx agree on every row. With only 2 possible rows, that is a complete proof.
Card 2. Absorption: x + xy = x: list every row of the variables (4 rows).
Fill each column from the definitions. The highlighted columns x, x+xy agree on every row. With only 4 possible rows, that is a complete proof.
Card 3. Redundant literal: x + x′y = x + y: list every row of the variables (4 rows).

set.text: Redundant literal: x + x′y = x + y

steps.caption: Fill each column from the definitions. The highlighted columns x+x′y, x+y agree on every row. With only 4 possible rows, that is a complete proof.

lfsr-feedback.title: A 3-bit LFSR stepping through 1, 2, 5, 3, 7, 6, 4
lfsr-feedback.intro: Three D flip-flops in a chain Q0 → Q1 → Q2 on one clock; an XOR of Q1 and Q2 feeds D0. The state is 4Q2 + 2Q1 + Q0. Each step is one clock edge.

steps.caption: Start at Q0 = 1, Q1 = Q2 = 0 (state 4Q2 + 2Q1 + Q0 = 1). The XOR of Q1 and Q2 is 0: that is what D0 will take at the next clock.
Clock 1: D0 took 0 (from the old Q1 ⊕ Q2), Q1 took Q0 and Q2 took Q1. State 010 = 2.
Clock 2: D0 took 1 (from the old Q1 ⊕ Q2), Q1 took Q0 and Q2 took Q1. State 101 = 5.
Clock 3: D0 took 1 (from the old Q1 ⊕ Q2), Q1 took Q0 and Q2 took Q1. State 011 = 3.
Clock 4: D0 took 1 (from the old Q1 ⊕ Q2), Q1 took Q0 and Q2 took Q1. State 111 = 7.
Clock 5: D0 took 0 (from the old Q1 ⊕ Q2), Q1 took Q0 and Q2 took Q1. State 110 = 6.
Clock 6: D0 took 0 (from the old Q1 ⊕ Q2), Q1 took Q0 and Q2 took Q1. State 100 = 4.
Clock 7: the state is 001 = 1 again. The cycle 1, 2, 5, 3, 7, 6, 4 visits all seven non-zero states.
The missing state is 000: there Q1 ⊕ Q2 = 0, so a 0 is fed in and the register stays at 000 forever. Seed an LFSR non-zero.

lockout-graph.title: Lock-out in the 0 → 3 → 5 → 6 JK counter
lockout-graph.intro: State graph of a 3-bit JK counter designed for 0 → 3 → 5 → 6 with the unused states as don't-cares. The main cycle is on the top row, the four unused states below; arcs appear as the circuit is simulated.

elements.text: The 0 → 3 → 5 → 6 JK counter: a lock-out and two cures

steps.caption: The 8 states ABC (A = MSB) of the counter built with J_A = K_A = Q_B, J_B = K_B = 1, J_C = K_C = Q_B′. Top row: the wanted cycle.
Simulating the circuit from 000 gives 000 → 011 → 101 → 110 → 000: the main cycle works exactly as designed.
Power up in 001 (B = 0): A holds, B toggles, C toggles, so next 010.
From 010 (B = 1): A toggles, B toggles, C holds, so 100.
From 100 (B = 0): A holds, B toggles, C toggles, so 111.
From 111 (B = 1): A toggles, B toggles, C holds, so 001. Back to 001: a lock-out cycle.
Cure 1 (forced next states): redesign with every unused state's next state set to 000. Each one now joins the cycle in one clock.
Cure 3 (another minimal cover), same cost: choose J_A = Q_C, K_A = Q_C′. Unused states: 001 → 110, 010 → 000, 100 → 011, 111 → 101.

set.text: every unused state enters the cycle
same main cycle, no extra gate

steps.caption: The lesson: don't-cares decide where unused states go. Always simulate all 2ⁿ states of the circuit you actually built.

set.text: check all 8 states, not just the 4 you wanted

master-slave.title: A master–slave D flip-flop: the master follows, the slave copies at the falling edge
master-slave.intro: Two D latches in series. The master is enabled by CLK, the slave by CLK through an inverter. Waveforms of CLK, D, the master M and Q grow half a period per step (delays ignored).

elements.text: Master–slave: two latches on opposite clock phases

steps.caption: CLK = 1: the master is open and follows D (M = 0 then 1); the slave is closed, so Q stays 0.
CLK falls: the master closes holding M = 1; the slave opens and copies it, so Q = 1. D changes now, but the master is shut.
CLK = 1: the master is open and follows D (M = 0 then 1 then 0); the slave is closed, so Q stays 1.
CLK falls: the master closes holding M = 0; the slave opens and copies it, so Q = 0. D changes now, but the master is shut.
CLK = 1: the master is open and follows D (M = 1); the slave is closed, so Q stays 0.
CLK falls: the master closes holding M = 1; the slave opens and copies it, so Q = 1. D changes now, but the master is shut.
CLK = 1: the master is open and follows D (M = 0 then 1); the slave is closed, so Q stays 1.
CLK falls: the master closes holding M = 1; the slave opens and copies it, so Q = 1. D changes now, but the master is shut.
Q moved only at the falling edges, each time to the value D had just before CLK fell: 1, 0, 1, 1.

set.text: never both open: an edge from two latches

mealy-moore-timing.title: Mealy and Moore output timing
mealy-moore-timing.intro: The overlapping 101 detector built twice, as a 3-state Mealy machine and a 4-state Moore machine, on one clock and one input x. Each step reveals one clock period; dashed lines are the rising edges; the state in each period is printed under its output.

elements.text: Mealy and Moore 101 detectors on the same input

steps.caption: One clock, one input x (applied just after each rising edge). Above: the Mealy 101 detector (3 states); below: the Moore one (4 states).
Period 1: x = 1. Mealy in S0, Moore in S0; no 101 has just ended, so both outputs are 0.

set.text: period 1: x = 1, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Period 2: x = 0. Mealy in S1, Moore in S1; no 101 has just ended, so both outputs are 0.

set.text: period 2: x = 0, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Period 3: in S2 the input 1 completes 101. The Mealy output goes high now, inside this period, before edge 3.

set.text: period 3: x = 1, z Mealy = 1, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Period 4: the Moore machine entered S3 at edge 3, so its output is high for this whole period: one clock after the Mealy output.

set.text: period 4: x = 1, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 1

steps.caption: Period 5: x = 0. Mealy in S1, Moore in S1; no 101 has just ended, so both outputs are 0.

set.text: period 5: x = 0, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Period 6: in S2 the input 1 completes 101. The Mealy output goes high now, inside this period, before edge 6.

set.text: period 6: x = 1, z Mealy = 1, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Period 7: the Moore machine entered S3 at edge 6, so its output is high for this whole period: one clock after the Mealy output.

set.text: period 7: x = 0, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 1

steps.caption: Period 8, in S2: a spike on x makes the Mealy output pulse. Edge 8 samples x = 0, so the state ignores it; the Moore output stays 0.

set.text: period 8: x = 0, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Period 9: x = 0. Mealy in S0, Moore in S0; no 101 has just ended, so both outputs are 0.

set.text: period 9: x = 0, z Mealy = 0, z Moore = 0

steps.caption: Same sequence, two timings: the Mealy output marks the period in which the last 1 arrives; the Moore output, the period after it.

minterm-highlighter.title: Expanding a sum of products into its minterms
minterm-highlighter.intro: f(P, Q, R) = PQ + QR′ + PR′. The rows are numbered with P as the most significant bit.

elements.text: From terms to minterms: each term lights its rows

steps.caption: The term PQ fixes 2 of the 3 variables, so it covers 2 rows: 110, 111, that is minterms 6 and 7.
The term QR′ fixes 2 of the 3 variables, so it covers 2 rows: 010, 110, that is minterms 2 and 6.
The term PR′ fixes 2 of the 3 variables, so it covers 2 rows: 100, 110, that is minterms 4 and 6.
f is the OR of the three columns: it is 1 wherever at least one term is 1. Row 6 is covered three times but is counted once.
Read the 1-rows of f: the canonical sum of products is Σm(2, 4, 6, 7), and the remaining rows give the product of maxterms ΠM(0, 1, 3, 5).

minterm-set-venn.title: AND, OR, XOR and NOT as set operations on minterm lists
minterm-set-venn.intro: Two functions of three variables, f = Σ(1, 3, 5, 7) and g = Σ(3, 6, 7), each drawn as the set of rows where it is 1.

steps.caption: AND keeps the rows that are in both sets: f·g = Σ(3, 7) (intersection).
OR keeps the rows in either set: f + g = Σ(1, 3, 5, 6, 7) (union).
XOR keeps the rows in exactly one set: f ⊕ g = Σ(1, 5, 6) (symmetric difference).
NOT keeps the rows outside the set: f′ = Σ(0, 2, 4, 6) (complement).

mod-n-clear.title: A mod-6 counter made by clearing a ripple counter at 110
mod-n-clear.intro: A 3-bit ripple up counter (one tick of delay per stage) whose flip-flops have an asynchronous clear driven by Q2 AND Q1. The waveforms grow one clock period per step; CLR is the gate output.

elements.text: Mod-6 from a 3-bit ripple counter: clear the moment 110 appears

steps.caption: A 3-bit ripple up counter whose flip-flops have an asynchronous clear. The AND gate watches Q2 and Q1, the 1 bits of 6 = 110.
Edge 1: the counter settles at 001 = 1. Q2 · Q1 = 0, so the clear stays inactive.
Edge 2: the counter settles at 010 = 2. Q2 · Q1 = 0, so the clear stays inactive.
Edge 3: the counter settles at 011 = 3. Q2 · Q1 = 0, so the clear stays inactive.
Edge 4: the counter settles at 100 = 4. Q2 · Q1 = 0, so the clear stays inactive.
Edge 5: the counter settles at 101 = 5. Q2 · Q1 = 0, so the clear stays inactive.
Edge 6: 101 → 100 → 110. Q2 = Q1 = 1, the gate fires and the clear wipes every stage to 000 within one clear delay.

set.text: 6 lives for one clear delay only

steps.caption: Edge 7: the counter settles at 001 = 1. Q2 · Q1 = 0, so the clear stays inactive.
The settled states are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then 0: a mod-6 counter. Detect N itself (not N − 1), because the clear acts at once.

msb-weight-bar.title: Place values of an 8-bit 2's-complement number
msb-weight-bar.intro: Eight bit cells with weights −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; the leftmost weight is negative. The pattern 10110100 has 1s under −128, 32, 16 and 4, so it is worth −76. The range is −128 to +127.

multi-output-sharing.title: Two outputs sharing a product term
multi-output-sharing.intro: Two functions of A, B, C to be built together; each map has rows A and columns B C.

elements.text: Two outputs, one shared product term

steps.caption: Minimise each output alone: f₁ = A′C + BC and f₂ = AB + BC. Built separately that is 4 AND gates (8 inputs) and 2 OR gates (4 inputs).
BC (m3, m7) appears in both answers. Build that AND gate once and send its output to both OR gates.

set.text: share BC: one gate, two fan-outs

steps.caption: Shared: 3 AND gates and 2 OR gates, 10 gate inputs. In multi-output design, look for product terms that can serve several outputs (Lesson 4 also shows a case where the shared term is not prime for either output).

set.text: f₁ = A′C + BC,  f₂ = AB + BC: 3 ANDs

mux-as-gates.title: A 2:1 multiplexer wired as NOT, AND, OR and NOR
mux-as-gates.intro: A 2:1 MUX outputs I0 when its select S is 0 and I1 when S is 1. Tying its inputs to constants and variables turns it into gates.

elements.text: A 2:1 MUX wired as NOT, AND, OR and NOR

steps.caption: NOT: put x on the select, 1 on I0 and 0 on I1. When x = 0 the MUX passes 1, when x = 1 it passes 0, so Y = x′.
AND: x on the select, 0 on I0, y on I1. When x = 0 the output is 0; when x = 1 it is y. So Y = x′·0 + x·y = xy.
OR: x on the select, y on I0, 1 on I1. When x = 0 the output is y; when x = 1 it is 1. So Y = x′y + x = x + y.
NOR needs two MUXes: MUX a (select y, inputs 1 and 0) makes y′; the second MUX (select x, inputs y′ and 0) gives Y = x′y′ = (x + y)′.
2:1 MUXes with 0 and 1 make NOT and AND, so they are complete. Read any constant cascade from its truth table: it may be NAND, not OR.

mux-cascade.title: Two cascaded 2:1 multiplexers evaluated row by row
mux-cascade.intro: MUX1 has inputs 0 and R with select P; its output M1 feeds input 1 of MUX2, whose input 0 is R′ and whose select is Q. The output is X.

elements.text: Two cascaded 2:1 MUXes (GATE 2016), row by row

steps.caption: P Q R = 0 0 0: MUX1 selects input 0 and passes 0, so M1 = 0; MUX2 selects input 0 and passes R′ = 1, so X = 1.
P Q R = 0 0 1: MUX1 selects input 0 and passes 0, so M1 = 0; MUX2 selects input 0 and passes R′ = 0, so X = 0.
P Q R = 0 1 0: MUX1 selects input 0 and passes 0, so M1 = 0; MUX2 selects input 1 and passes M1 = 0, so X = 0.
P Q R = 0 1 1: MUX1 selects input 0 and passes 0, so M1 = 0; MUX2 selects input 1 and passes M1 = 0, so X = 0.
P Q R = 1 0 0: MUX1 selects input 1 and passes R = 0, so M1 = 0; MUX2 selects input 0 and passes R′ = 1, so X = 1.
P Q R = 1 0 1: MUX1 selects input 1 and passes R = 1, so M1 = 1; MUX2 selects input 0 and passes R′ = 0, so X = 0.
P Q R = 1 1 0: MUX1 selects input 1 and passes R = 0, so M1 = 0; MUX2 selects input 1 and passes M1 = 0, so X = 0.
P Q R = 1 1 1: MUX1 selects input 1 and passes R = 1, so M1 = 1; MUX2 selects input 1 and passes M1 = 1, so X = 1.
X = 1 only on rows 000, 100, 111 (minterms 0, 4, 7). MUX1 gives M1 = PR, so X = Q′R′ + Q·PR: the minimal SOP is Q′R′ + PQR.

mux-enable-expand.title: An 8-to-1 multiplexer from two enabled 4-to-1 multiplexers
mux-enable-expand.intro: Two 4:1 MUXes with enable inputs: MUX A holds I0–I3, MUX B holds I4–I7. S2 picks the MUX through the enables; an OR joins the outputs.

elements.text: An 8:1 MUX from two 4:1 MUXes with enables
S1 S0 go to both MUXes

steps.caption: Two 4:1 MUXes share S1 S0. MUX A takes I0–I3 and is enabled by S2′; MUX B takes I4–I7 and is enabled by S2.
S2 S1 S0 = 010: S2 = 0 enables MUX A, which passes its input 2 (I2 = 1); MUX B outputs 0. Y = 1.
S2 S1 S0 = 110: S2 = 1 enables MUX B, which passes its input 2 (I6 = 0); MUX A outputs 0. Y = 0.
S2 S1 S0 = 101: S2 = 1 enables MUX B, which passes its input 1 (I5 = 0); MUX A outputs 0. Y = 0.
S2 S1 S0 = 011: S2 = 0 enables MUX A, which passes its input 3 (I3 = 0); MUX B outputs 0. Y = 0.
Y = S2′·MUX A + S2·MUX B: a disabled MUX outputs 0, so the OR passes the enabled one. Two 4:1 MUXes and an OR make an 8:1.

mux-implement.title: Implementing a function on a 4:1 MUX with an implementation table
mux-implement.intro: f(x, y, z) = Σ(0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6) goes on a 4:1 MUX with y and z on the selects. The implementation table finds what each data input must be.

elements.text: Implementing Σ(0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6) on a 4:1 MUX (selects y, z)

steps.caption: Row x′ holds minterms 0–3 (x = 0), row x holds 4–7; each column is one value of yz. Ring row x′'s 1s: 0, 1, 3.
Ring the 1s of row x: 4, 5 and 6. Now read each column: which rows are ringed decides that data input.
Column yz = 00 (minterms 0 and 4): both minterms are 1, so the input is 1 whatever x is. I0 = 1.
Column yz = 01 (minterms 1 and 5): both minterms are 1, so the input is 1 whatever x is. I1 = 1.
Column yz = 10 (minterms 2 and 6): only the x row is ringed, so the input equals x. I2 = x.
Column yz = 11 (minterms 3 and 7): only the x′ row is ringed, so the input equals x′. I3 = x′.
Wire the residues: I0 = 1, I1 = 1, I2 = x, I3 = x′, y on S1, z on S0. One 4:1 MUX plus an inverter realises f.
Check minterm 6 (x y z = 1 1 0): the selects pick I2 = x = 1, so f = 1; 6 is in the list.
Check minterm 7 (x y z = 1 1 1): the selects pick I3 = x′ = 0, so f = 0; 7 is not in the list.

mux-latch.title: A multiplexer with feedback is a D latch
mux-latch.intro: A 2:1 multiplexer: data input 1 is D, data input 0 is the output Q fed back, select is S. Waveforms of S, D and Q grow below.

elements.text: A 2:1 MUX with its output fed back to input 0

steps.caption: Ticks 0–1: S = 0, so the MUX passes its own output back: Q keeps its value whatever D does.

set.text: S = 0: input 0 is Q itself, so Q holds

steps.caption: Ticks 2–3: S = 1, so the MUX passes D and Q copies it one MUX delay later.
Ticks 4–5: S = 1, so the MUX passes D and Q copies it one MUX delay later.
Ticks 6–7: S = 1, so the MUX passes D and Q copies it one MUX delay later.
Ticks 8–9: S = 0, so the MUX passes its own output back: Q keeps its value whatever D does.

set.text: S = 0: input 0 is Q itself, so Q holds

steps.caption: Ticks 10–11: S = 0, so the MUX passes its own output back: Q keeps its value whatever D does.

set.text: S = 0: input 0 is Q itself, so Q holds

steps.caption: Ticks 12–13: S = 0, so the MUX passes its own output back: Q keeps its value whatever D does.

set.text: S = 0: input 0 is Q itself, so Q holds

steps.caption: Ticks 14–15: S = 1, so the MUX passes D and Q copies it one MUX delay later.
Ticks 16–17: S = 1, so the MUX passes D and Q copies it one MUX delay later.
Ticks 18–19: S = 0, so the MUX passes its own output back: Q keeps its value whatever D does.

set.text: S = 0: input 0 is Q itself, so Q holds

steps.caption: Ticks 20–21: S = 0, so the MUX passes its own output back: Q keeps its value whatever D does.

set.text: S = 0: input 0 is Q itself, so Q holds

steps.caption: Transparent while S = 1, holding while S = 0, level-sensitive, not edge-sensitive: a D latch (GATE 2023, option B).

set.text: Q⁺ = S·D + S̄·Q: a D latch

mux-routing.title: A 4:1 multiplexer routing the selected input to its output
mux-routing.intro: A 4:1 MUX with data inputs I0 I1 I2 I3 = 0 1 1 0. The select lines S1 S0 choose which input reaches Y.

elements.text: A 4:1 MUX routes one data input to Y

steps.caption: Select S1S0 = 00: input I0 (value 0) is routed to Y, so Y = 0.
Select S1S0 = 01: input I1 (value 1) is routed to Y, so Y = 1.
Select S1S0 = 10: input I2 (value 1) is routed to Y, so Y = 1.
Select S1S0 = 11: input I3 (value 0) is routed to Y, so Y = 0.
Over the four selects Y reads 0 1 1 0: the data inputs are the truth table, so Y = S1 ⊕ S0.

mux-tree.title: A 16:1 multiplexer built as a tree of 4:1 multiplexers
mux-tree.intro: Sixteen data inputs I0–I15 must reach one output Y using only 4:1 multiplexers. The tree is built level by level.

elements.text: A 16:1 MUX from 4:1 MUXes, level by level

steps.caption: Level 1: ⌈16 / 4⌉ = 4 blocks of 4:1, each taking four of the sixteen data inputs (I0–I3, I4–I7, I8–I11, I12–I15).
The low select bits S1 S0 go to every first-level block, so all four pick the input in the same position.
Level 2: ⌈4 / 4⌉ = 1 block takes the four first-level outputs; the high select bits S3 S2 choose which block's output reaches Y.
Select S3S2S1S0 = 1001: S1S0 = 01 makes each first-level block pass its input 1 (I1, I5, I9, I13); S3S2 = 10 passes block 2, so Y = I9.
Select S3S2S1S0 = 0110: S1S0 = 10 makes each first-level block pass its input 2 (I2, I6, I10, I14); S3S2 = 01 passes block 1, so Y = I6.
Total: 4 + 1 = 5 MUXes in 2 levels. Each level divides the count by 4 and rounds up; for a full tree the total is (16 − 1)/(4 − 1) = 5.

nand-builds.title: Building NOT, AND and OR from NAND gates
nand-builds.intro: NAND gates only. Three small circuits will appear, one per basic gate.

elements.text: Everything from NAND: NOT, AND and OR

steps.caption: NOT: tie both inputs of a NAND together. NAND(x, x) = (x·x)′ = x′. One gate.
AND: a NAND followed by a NAND used as an inverter undoes the inversion: ((AB)′)′ = AB. Two gates.
OR: invert both inputs, then NAND them: (A′·B′)′ = A + B by De Morgan. Three gates.
NOT, AND and OR can build every function (canonical SOP), so NAND alone can build every function: it is universal. The NOR gate is the dual: NOT 1, OR 2, AND 3.

nand-latch.title: The NAND SR latch: active-low inputs and its forbidden 00
nand-latch.intro: Two NAND gates, cross-coupled. The inputs S̄ and R̄ are active low: a 0 sets or resets. Waveforms grow below, one column per gate delay.

elements.text: The NAND latch: active-low inputs S̄ and R̄

steps.caption: S̄ = 0 (a 0 does the work): Q = NAND(0, Q̄) = 1, then Q̄ = NAND(1, 1) = 0. Set: Q = 1.
S̄ = R̄ = 1: the inputs are idle and the loop holds Q = 1. For a NAND latch, 11 is hold.
R̄ = 0: Q̄ = NAND(0, Q) = 1, then Q = NAND(1, 1) = 0. Reset: Q = 0.
S̄ = R̄ = 1 again: hold Q = 0.
S̄ = R̄ = 0: both NANDs see a 0, so Q = Q̄ = 1 (GATE 2004: Q = 1, Q′ = 1, not 'indeterminate').
Both go back to 1 together (00 → 11, IT 2007): each gate sees 1, 1 and falls, then rises: oscillation.
NAND latch: 11 holds, 01 sets, 10 resets, 00 is forbidden. It is the NOR latch with every input level inverted.

set.text: 00 → 11 races, like 11 → 00 on a NOR latch

nand-nand-conversion.title: Converting AND–OR into NAND–NAND
nand-nand-conversion.intro: A sum of products, F = AB + CD, built as AND gates feeding an OR gate.

elements.text: AND–OR to NAND–NAND by bubble pairs

steps.caption: Start from the two-level AND–OR circuit for F = AB + CD: one AND per product term, one OR to combine them.
Put a bubble at the output of each AND and a bubble at the matching OR input. Each wire now has two bubbles, which cancel, so the function is unchanged.
An OR with bubbled inputs is a NAND (De Morgan). Redraw it: the whole circuit is now NAND–NAND.
Rule: any two-level AND–OR (sum of products) becomes NAND–NAND by replacing every gate with a NAND. A single-literal term must first pass through an inverter.

nand-nand-from-kmap.title: From a minimal SOP to a NAND–NAND circuit
nand-nand-from-kmap.intro: f(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7) on a 3-variable map (rows A, columns B C); complemented inputs are available.

elements.text: From a K-map to a NAND–NAND circuit

steps.caption: Loop the map: A′C (m1, m3) and AB (m6, m7). The minimal SOP is f = A′C + AB.
Each loop becomes an AND gate fed by its literals (A′ is available as an input), and the OR gate collects the loops: a two-level AND–OR circuit.

set.text: loops → AND gates, sum → OR gate

steps.caption: Put two bubbles on each wire between the levels (a double inversion changes nothing). An AND with an output bubble is a NAND; an OR with input bubbles is, by De Morgan, a NAND.

set.text: add bubble pairs on the middle wires

steps.caption: So the same circuit is three NAND gates: f = NAND(NAND(A′, C), NAND(A, B)). Every SOP becomes NAND–NAND this way; a POS becomes NOR–NOR dually.

negate-invert-plus-one.title: Invert and add 1, and the copy-to-the-first-1 shortcut
negate-invert-plus-one.intro: The 8-bit pattern of +88: 01011000. We will build the pattern of −88 underneath.

elements.text: Negating +88 in 8 bits: invert, then add 1

steps.caption: Flip every bit of 01011000. The result 10100111 is x̄, and x + x̄ = 11111111 = 2⁸ − 1.
Add 1 to x̄. The three trailing 1s of x̄ turn into 0s as the carry ripples left, and the first 0 it meets becomes 1.
Compare x and −x: the rightmost 1 of x and everything to its right (1000) are copied unchanged; every bit to its left is flipped. That is the copy-to-the-first-1 shortcut.
Check: 10101000 read with the −128 weight is −128 + 32 + 8 = −88.

normalise-shift.title: Normalising a significand: shift left, lower the exponent
normalise-shift.intro: The significand 0.0001011 times 2 to the 6 is 5.5, but it starts with three zeros after the point, which waste precision.

elements.label: not normalised: three 0s after the point

steps.caption: Find the first 1. It sits in the 4th place after the point, so the significand starts with three wasted zeros.
Fraction form (0.1…): shift the significand 3 places left, so the first 1 sits just after the point. A left shift by 3 multiplies by 2³, so the exponent drops by 3: 0.1011 × 2³.
Hidden-bit form (1.f): shift one more place, so the first 1 sits before the point. The exponent drops once more: 1.011 × 2².
In the hidden-bit form the bit before the point is always 1, so it is not stored. The fraction field keeps only 011 (then zeros), and every shift kept the value at 5.5.

octal-hex-bridge.title: The binary bridge from octal to hex
